corrected_value.title: Different stories: How levels of familiarity with literary and genre fiction relate to mentalizing.

decisions.location: Results, Additional analyses: Replication and extension of Kidd and Castano (2017a) (lines 1035-1046); Table 10 (lines 884-931); Conclusions (lines 1105-1108); References (lines 1228-1231)
decisions.quote:
Replication and extension of Kidd and Castano (2017a). The
present data afford the opportunity to replicate and extend correlational findings concerning the relations of familiarity with
literary and genre authors included on the ART and performance on the RMET (Kidd & Castano, 2017a). Literary and
genre fiction familiarity scores were calculated as described
in Kidd and Castano (2017a) and square-root transformed.
Following Kidd and Castano (2017a), guessing scores on
the ART were included as a covariate in the models regressing
the ToM measures on literary and genre familiarity scores (see
Table 10). In the model testing effects on the MJT, baseline
judgment scores were also included as a covariate. For both

ToM measures, familiarity with literary authors positively predicted performance, but familiarity with genre authors did not.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. Full-text review of 05781ebeec482e07.txt (Kidd & Castano, 2018, 10.1177/1948550618775410) establishes all three required facts for target_index 1: (1) Actual empirical retesting of a specific published finding: In addition to experimentally retesting Experiment 5 of Kidd and Castano (2013) (target_index 0), the authors include a dedicated Results subsection titled 'Replication and extension of Kidd and Castano (2017a)' and Table 10 ('Literary and Genre Author Familiarity as Predictors of RMET and MJT Performance'), computing square-root-transformed literary and genre author familiarity scores from the Author Recognition Test (ART) across all three new experiments (Experiments 1, 2, and 3; N = 305, 318, and 346) and regressing Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET) and Moral Judgment Task (MJT) performance on literary and genre familiarity controlling for ART guessing scores, concluding both in Results and in Conclusions ('replicated in each of the three present studies') that familiarity with literary authors positively predicted Theory of Mind (ToM) performance whereas familiarity with genre authors did not. (2) Source-backed original identity: Explicitly cited as Kidd and Castano (2017a) and listed in the References (lines 1228-1231) as 'Kidd, D., & Castano, E. (2017a). Different stories: How levels of familiarity with literary and genre fiction relate to mentalizing. Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts, 11, 474–486. doi:10.1037/aca0000069' (also verified in bibliography_metadata.json). (3) Absence and non-equivalence against all shipped rows: The sole shipped row for this work is input_row_index 483 (Kidd & Castano, 2013, 'Reading Literary Fiction Improves Theory of Mind', Science, 10.1126/science.1239918), which matches sibling target_index 0. Report equivalence does not apply because Kidd and Castano (2013) reports short-term experimental manipulations of reading assigned literary vs. popular fiction texts, whereas Kidd and Castano (2017) is a separate later article reporting correlational studies of lifetime familiarity with literary vs. genre fiction authors on the ART.
